extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of public opinion and political communication; political practitioners crafting public appeals
extracted.subtask_short: crafting public appeals and political symbols
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing public appeals, speeches, and policy statements that can unite diverse publics — covering choice and phrasing of symbols, timing and messengers, use of specificity versus vagueness, and designing statements to satisfy multiple constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heal party schisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The speaker must heal [a schism] — remind divergent factions of their common history and avoid dwelling on the schism itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Lincoln's appeal to Republicans, Bull Moose and Old Guard — do not speak of the schism; speaker's task is to restore a sense of common past so factions will unite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a non-explosive opening subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Find an opening subject which will not only ignore past schisms but will avoid explosive conflicts; choose a subject that can create a common mood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Hughes selected the spoils system in diplomatic appointments as an 'ideal introduction to a common mood' — the topic must be defensible and allow vigorous attack without reawakening toxic divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specificity on factual records to avoid arousing contrary passions
rubrics_metrics.description: On non-contentious matters use specific facts and detailed recounting to avoid provoking contrary passions; specificity can confine controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Listing concrete incidents (Tampico, Vera Cruz, Villa, Columbus, Carrizal) keeps the record non-contentious; but even then a candidate may be forced to take a position because audiences expect it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ strategic vagueness but recognise its costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Vagueness at a crucial point in public debate is usually a symptom of cross-purposes; obscurantism in public appeals often results when superficial harmony is the aim and conflict the fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While stretching words to mean 'all things to all men' can repress contentious issues and unite factions temporarily, it disperses meaning and can conceal unresolved conflicts — beware that vagueness can backfire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use broad symbols to amalgamate conflicting emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols (Americanism, Progressivism, Law and Order, Justice, Humanity) are used to amalgamate the emotion of conflicting factions which would divide if asked to discuss specific programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such symbolic phrases do not stand for specific ideas but serve as a 'truce or junction between ideas'; they enable coalition-building by shifting feeling toward conformity rather than critical scrutiny of measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earmark symbols through authoritative messengers and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols must be 'earmarked' — they must be spoken by people who are strategically placed and at the opportune moment; otherwise they are mere wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A symbol gains power because it is introduced by congenial and important people; selection of the messenger and timing is essential to implanting the symbol in people's minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit conditioned responses: find a shared stimulus
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of 'conditioned response, an emotion is not attached merely to one idea' — find or create a stimulus which will arouse the same emotion in many different groups to unite them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: If one person dislikes the League, another hates Wilson, a third fears labor, a common antithesis (e.g., 'Americanism') can be used so each reads their own meaning into the same symbol and feel united.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft phrasing to satisfy multiple contingencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose wording so it meets diverse expectations without committing to a single contested outcome; choose words that are precise enough to signal intent but flexible enough to cover contingencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In the Fourteen Points the phrase 'the wrong done to France by Prussia in 1871 ... should be righted' was chosen instead of 'Alsace-Lorraine should be restored' to leave room for plebiscite outcomes and allied contingencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design public documents to unify yet remain flexible
rubrics_metrics.description: Public statements intended to rally broad support should be structured to hold interest 'unified and flexible' across different possibilities; they must meet national aspirations while limiting them so no one nation becomes a catspaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Wilson numbered the Fourteen Points to secure precision and give a business-like appearance; terms were intended to meet official and popular interests and to be 'terms of a possible peace' so they could function in multiple scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of substituting names for objects (guard against verbalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: When people simplify and use shorthand names and signs they may 'talk about names regardless of objects' — this verbalism disconnects discourse from reality and leads to mistaken associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep in mind the original referents of words; guard against 'changeling' substitutions where a name divorced from its object begins to mismatch other things it is associated with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of symbols; avoid overuse/abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols have limits and can 'burst' under abuse or excessive resistance to new purposes; overextending what a symbol is taken to represent destroys its unifying power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The symbol of Holy Russia and the Little Father 'burst' under suffering and defeat in 1917 — monitor tolerance for abuse and evolve or retire symbols when they no longer fit reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand tradeoff: broader coalition reduces intellectual specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: As one ascends a hierarchy of symbols to include more factions, emotional connection may be preserved while intellectual content and specificity are lost; broader appeal often sacrifices detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate about how far to generalize: higher-level phrases ('Rights of Humanity') can unite many but mean very little concretely; expect divergent private meanings to be projected onto such phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer symbols rooted in experience over omnibus abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'true symbol' that has genuine contact with people's experience endures; an 'omnibus' abstraction creates only transient harmony and lacks emotional depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and local attachments (e.g., 'France' as a symbol) can be more durable and mobilizing than recent, broad abstractions like 'Europe' which may lack deep roots in constituents' imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select trustworthy authorities to translate distant facts
rubrics_metrics.description: When facts are 'out of sight' people choose between trustworthy and untrustworthy reporters; since most cannot assess truth directly, the choice of credible experts or authoritative figures is central to shaping opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice pick accessible and recognizable authorities (parents, teachers, public personages) who can serve as bridges to unfamiliar environments; diversifying authorities can approximate independence when full scrutiny is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallize common will via strategic leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of forming a common will often requires a strategic actor ('an Alexander Hamilton at work') who can see beyond local attachments and fashion national-level symbols and compromises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders who lack primitive local attachments may be able to trade local priorities for national gains (e.g., Hamilton trading the capital site for assumption of state debts); recognize the role of such strategists in coalition formation.
